What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dict from character to the last index where it appeared
You need O(1) lookup of 'where did I last see this value?'
O(1) membership test on the dict keys
Checking for a repeat without scanning the window
You need the index and the item in the same loop
Keeps the largest window length seen so far

p: Input `"abcabcbb"`. `l` is the left edge of the window and `r` the right edge. The window always holds distinct characters.

blocks.h: Why `seen[ch] >= l` and not just `ch in seen`?
p: `seen` is never cleaned, so it can remember a character from before the window start. Such a stale entry must not move `l` backwards or forwards. Trace of `"abba"`:
bullets: At `r=3` the second `a` was last seen at index 0, which is already left of `l=2`, so it is not a repeat inside the window.
Without the `>= l` check, `l` would jump back to 1 and the window `"ba"` would wrongly become `"bba"`.
Time: O(n). `r` moves once across the string and `l` only ever moves right (it never goes backward), so no character is processed more than twice.
Space: O(min(n, alphabet size)) for the dict.

3.takeaway: Sliding window with a last-seen index map: expand `r` every step and jump `l` straight past a repeated character instead of shrinking one step at a time.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A list of numRows empty strings, one per zigzag row
You build several output lines side by side
Appends the character to row r
Distributing characters into buckets as you scan
Direction flag: down or up the rows
Bouncing back and forth between two boundaries
Concatenates the rows top to bottom
Joining a list of strings in one pass (cheaper than repeated +=)

p: `s = "PAYPALISHIRING"`, `numRows = 3`. `r` is the row the character goes into, `d` the direction used after placing it.

blocks.h: Why check the direction at both ends?
p: The direction flips only at the top row (`r == 0`) and the bottom row (`r == numRows - 1`). In between it keeps its value, which is what makes the path a zigzag rather than a sweep.
`numRows == 1` is handled first because with one row `r` is both the top and the bottom, so `d` would flip every step and `r` would leave the list.

bullets: Time: O(n) for one pass over the string (plus the join).
Space: O(n) for the row strings.

p: The code never computes row positions with math. It simulates the walk, so there is no cycle-length formula (`2 * numRows - 2`) to get off by one.

6.takeaway: Simulate the zigzag with a row pointer and a direction flag that flips at the two boundaries, then join the rows.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Peeling digits off the right end
Shrinking a number one digit at a time
Appends that digit to the end of rev
Building a reversed number without strings
Drops the middle digit of rev (odd-length case)
Comparing halves when length may be odd

p: The loop stops once the reversed half is at least as large as what remains of `x`, so only half the digits are reversed.
`x = 12321` (odd length):
bullets: Stop: `x = 12`, `rev = 123`. Not equal, but `rev // 10 = 12 == x`, so the middle digit `3` is ignored: palindrome.
Stop: `x == rev == 12`: palindrome.

blocks.h: Why the early return for trailing zeros?
p: A number ending in 0 can only be a palindrome if it is 0, because a palindrome would need to start with 0. Without the guard the loop wrongly accepts `10`: `x=10` gives `x=1, rev=0`, continues to `x=0, rev=1`, and then `x == rev // 10` is `0 == 0`. Running the code with the guard removed returns `True` for `10`.

bullets: Time: O(log10 n), one step per half of the digits.
Space: O(1). No string conversion, which is the point of this version.

9.takeaway: Reverse only the second half of the digits and compare with the first half; stopping at the midpoint avoids overflow and extra space.

The mapping has special cases that you want as data, not as if-branches

p: `num = 1994`. Only the rows where a symbol was used are shown.

Listing 900, 400, 90, 40, 9, 4 as their own entries turns the subtractive rule into plain greedy choice: at every point the largest value that fits is always the right one, because the list is ordered and contains every legal symbol group.
Without the six subtractive entries, 4 would come out as `IIII` and 1994 as `MDCCCCLXXXXIIII`.

bullets: Time: O(1). The output has a bounded length (at most 15 symbols for inputs up to 3999) and the table has 13 entries.
Space: O(1).

12.takeaway: Greedy over a descending value table where the subtractive forms are extra rows; this turns a rule-heavy conversion into a simple loop.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sorts in place in O(n log n)
You want two pointers or easy duplicate skipping
Detects a repeated anchor value (valid only because the array is sorted)
Two pointers closing in from both ends of the rest of the array
A sorted array and a target sum

p: Sorted input `[-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]`. `i` is the anchor, `l` and `r` the pointers.

blocks.h: Why does moving a pointer work?
p: Because the array is sorted, a sum that is too small can only grow by moving `l` right, and a sum that is too large can only shrink by moving `r` left. Every skipped pair is provably unable to reach 0, so the inner loop is O(n) instead of O(n²).

After finding a triplet, `l` skips past equal values (`while ... nums[l] == nums[l-1]`) so the same triplet is not reported twice. The anchor skip (`i and nums[i] == nums[i-1]`) removes duplicates for `i`.

bullets: Time: O(n²): n anchors times an O(n) two-pointer sweep. The sort is O(n log n) and does not dominate.
Space: O(1) extra besides the output (ignoring the sort's internal space).

15.takeaway: Sort, fix one number, then use two converging pointers on the rest; skip equal values to avoid duplicate triplets.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Orders the array in place, O(n log n)
Two-pointer sum search and duplicate skipping both need sorted order
Bounds that leave room for the two pointers after j
Avoiding index checks inside the loops
Skips repeated values at that level; `j > i + 1` stops it from comparing against `nums[i]`
Sorted array, find pairs hitting a target

p: Sorted `[-2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2]`, target 0. Columns 1–4 are the four chosen numbers.

The duplicate check at level j must only compare with the previous value that was also tried as j for this i. Index `i + 1` is the first j for this i, so it has no previous sibling. With `j > 0` the first j would be skipped whenever it equals `nums[i]`, which would drop valid answers such as `[0, 0, 0, 0]` or `[-2, -2, 2, 2]`.

bullets: Time: O(n³): two nested loops times an O(n) pointer sweep. For k-Sum this generalizes to O(n^(k-1)).
Space: O(1) extra besides the output and the sort.

18.takeaway: k-Sum is sort, fix k-2 numbers with duplicate skips, then close the last two with converging pointers.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dummy node placed before the head
The head itself can change (here the first pair moves)
Node just before the current pair
Both nodes of a pair exist
a.next = b.next; b.next = a; prev.next = b
Three pointer writes that swap the pair in place
After the swap `a` is the second node of the pair, so it is the new predecessor

p: `1→2→3→4`. Each step swaps the pair `(a, b)` and the table shows the list from the head afterwards.

blocks.h: Why this order of the three writes?
p: `a.next = b.next` goes first so the rest of the list (`3→4`) is saved before `b.next` is overwritten. Then `b.next = a` points b back at a, and `prev.next = b` hooks the swapped pair into the list. Doing `b.next = a` first would lose the node after b.

bullets: Time: O(n), one pass.
Space: O(1); the nodes are relinked, not copied.

p: The loop condition checks `prev.next` before `prev.next.next`; with an odd count the final single node is simply left in place.

24.takeaway: Pointer surgery with a dummy head: save the tail of the pair first, then reverse the pair and reconnect the predecessor.

In-place filtering; the 'slow and fast pointer' pattern
Overwrites the slot at k with a kept value
New logical length; the contents beyond k don't matter

blocks.h: Why is it safe to overwrite while reading?
p: `k` never gets ahead of the read position (it advances at most once per element read), so an overwrite only ever touches a slot that has already been read.

bullets: Time: O(n) with a single pass.
Space: O(1); no extra array.

p: The order of the kept elements is preserved. If the number of elements to remove is tiny, swapping with the last element writes less, but this version is simpler and stable.

27.takeaway: Read pointer scans, write pointer collects the survivors: the standard in-place filter.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Word length and word count; every word has the same length
Fixed-size chunks make the total window length `w * n`
Multiset of required words, as word → count
Comparing 'same items, any order'; handles repeated words
Every start position where a full window fits
The j-th word-sized chunk inside the window
Cutting a string into equal pieces
Counters compare by contents, ignoring order

p: `s = "barfoothefoobarman"`, `words = ["foo", "bar"]`, window length 6:

blocks.h: Why a Counter and not a set or a sorted compare?
bullets: A set ignores counts. With `words = ["foo", "foo", "bar"]` the window chunks `["foo", "bar", "bar"]` give the same set `{foo, bar}` and would be accepted wrongly.
Counter equality keeps multiplicities and ignores order, which is exactly 'every word used exactly once, any order'.

Time: O((len(s) − w·n + 1) · n · w): each window builds a Counter from n chunks of length w (hashing a chunk costs O(w)). This is the simple version; a sliding window per offset reaches O(len(s) · w).
Space: O(n · w) for the Counter.

30.takeaway: Fixed-width window with a Counter comparison; the Counter handles duplicates and order-independence in one equality check.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Halving a range; Python ints don't overflow
Tests which half is sorted. `<=` matters when lo == mid
Binary search on a rotated array
Range test: is the target inside the sorted half?

blocks.h: Why check which half is sorted first?
p: After rotation, comparing the target with `nums[mid]` alone says nothing about the side. But one half is always fully sorted, and in a sorted half a range check (`nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]`) is reliable. If the target is not in the sorted half it must be in the other, so one comparison always eliminates half the array.

Why `<=` in `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`? When `lo == mid` (a one- or two-element range) the left 'half' is a single element, which is sorted; using `<` would send that case to the right-half branch and mis-handle it.

bullets: Time: O(log n) because every iteration halves the range.
Space: O(1).
Distinct values are required: with duplicates `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` can't tell which half is sorted (that is problem 81).

33.takeaway: Modified binary search: at each step one half is sorted, so test whether the target lies in it and discard the other half.

Three tuple keys per cell: value v in row r, in column c, in box (r//3, c//3). The leading tag keeps the three namespaces apart
One set standing in for 27 sets; tuples are hashable
Maps 9×9 coordinates to one of the 3×3 boxes
any(k in seen for k in keys)
True as soon as one of the three keys exists
Adds all three keys at once

p: On the standard example board, the first cells of row 0 and row 1 add these keys (no clashes, so the board stays valid):

If the top-left `5` is replaced by `8`, the scan reaches cell `(2,2)` with value `8`. The check finds this key already in `seen`: `[('b', 0, 0, '8')]`. The function returns False immediately; remaining cells are never read.

Without the tag, `(0, '5')` could mean either 'row 0 holds a 5' or 'column 0 holds a 5'. A 5 in row 0 and a different 5 in column 0 is perfectly legal, but untagged keys would collide and report a false duplicate. The tag keeps the three constraint families apart.

bullets: Time: O(81), constant, since the board is fixed at 9×9 (O(n²) for an n×n generalization).
Space: O(81) keys at most, constant.

36.takeaway: Validate with one hash set of tagged keys (row, column, box) and stop at the first duplicate.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Two pointers moving inward from the ends
Each step depends on the smaller of two ends
Tallest bar seen so far from the left and from the right
Water above bar l: the wall level minus the bar's height (never negative because lmax ≥ height[l])
Computing a per-position quantity from a bound

p: The classic input `[0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1]`, total water 6. Each row processes one bar:

blocks.h: Why is it safe to use only the smaller side?
p: Water above a bar is `min(left wall, right wall) − height`. If `height[l] < height[r]`, the left side is the limiting one. `lmax` is the exact left wall for `l`. The true right wall is at least `lmax`: every left bar passed so far was smaller than the bar at `r` at that moment, and that bar (or a taller one) still lies to the right of `l`. So the water at `l` is exactly `lmax − height[l]`, whatever sits between `l` and `r`. The same argument applies symmetrically on the right.

bullets: Time: O(n), each bar is processed once.
Space: O(1). The prefix/suffix-array version needs O(n); the two pointers fold those arrays into two variables.

42.takeaway: Two pointers from both ends, always processing the lower side, because the lower wall alone decides the water level there.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Furthest index reachable from any position seen so far in this layer
Greedy 'how far can I get' reasoning
Right edge of the range reachable with `jumps` jumps
Reached the edge of the current layer, so another jump is required
Stops before the last index; at the last index no jump is needed

blocks.h: Why is this a BFS in disguise?
p: Positions reachable in k jumps form a contiguous range, so a layer of BFS is just `(previous cur_end, cur_end]`. `far` is the farthest the next layer can reach. When `i` passes the layer's edge, one more jump is paid and the next layer begins. No queue is needed because the layer is an interval.

bullets: Time: O(n), single pass.
Space: O(1).
Assumes the end is reachable (the problem guarantees it). Without that guarantee `far` could stay equal to `i` and the answer would be wrong.

p: The loop excludes the last index on purpose: if `cur_end` were exactly `n − 1` and the loop included it, an unnecessary extra jump would be counted.

45.takeaway: Greedy BFS over intervals: count a jump each time you pass the boundary of what the current jump count can reach.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Visits only the cells above the diagonal, so every pair is swapped once
Transposing in place; starting at 0 would swap twice and undo itself
Reverses a list in place, O(n)
Mirroring a row; `row[::-1]` would create a copy and not change the matrix

p: A clockwise rotation equals transpose, then reverse every row:

The cell at row i, column j must end up at row j, column n−1−i. Transpose moves it to (j, i); reversing each row maps column i to n−1−i. The anticlockwise version reverses columns first (or transposes along the other diagonal).

bullets: Time: O(n²), each cell is touched a constant number of times.
Space: O(1); the matrix is modified in place as required.

48.takeaway: Rotate 90° clockwise = transpose + reverse each row; both steps are in place.

What it does

Occupied columns, '\' diagonals and '/' diagonals; O(1) conflict test
Avoiding a scan of every placed queen
Constant along a '\' diagonal, so it identifies that diagonal
Column chosen for each row so far (row = index)
Builds one board row as text from the column index
Rendering results lazily at the end

p: `n = 4`. Rows are placed one per recursion level, the list shows the column of the queen in each row. Events until the first solution is found (there are two solutions in total, the second appears after more backtracking):

Each recursion level handles one row, so two queens can never share a row. Only columns and diagonals need checking, and the three sets make each check O(1). The backtracking removes the queen's entries from all three sets, so the sets always reflect only the current partial placement.

bullets: Time: roughly O(n!) in the worst case; pruning by the three sets cuts it dramatically in practice.
Space: O(n) for the recursion, the sets and `board`, plus the output.

51.takeaway: Backtracking row by row with three sets (column, diagonal, anti-diagonal) for O(1) conflict checks.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Removes and returns the first row (O(rows) because the list shifts)
Transposes: `*m` unpacks the rows as arguments, `zip` groups the i-th item of each
zip gives tuples; this converts them back to lists
Needed because later `pop(0)` and `+=` expect lists
Reverses the order of the rows
Combined with a transpose: rotate 90° counter-clockwise
Extends the result list in place

p: `[[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]`. Each loop takes the top row, then rotates what is left counter-clockwise so that the next unvisited edge (the right column) becomes the new top row.

blocks.h: Why does transpose + reverse make the next side the top row?
p: After removing the top row, the right-hand column should be read top to bottom next. Transposing makes that column the last row; reversing the row order moves it to the first row, ready for `pop(0)`. Each iteration therefore repeats the same simple step, turning a spiral into repeated 'take the top row'.

bullets: Time: roughly O(n·m·(n+m)) as written: there are up to n+m rounds and each rebuilds the remaining matrix. It is short rather than optimal; the four-boundary walk is O(n·m).
Space: O(n·m) for the rebuilt matrix each round.

54.takeaway: Peel the top row, rotate the rest counter-clockwise with zip(*m)[::-1], repeat: elegant but costlier than boundary pointers.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Interval ends strictly before the new one starts, so no overlap
Classifying an interval as 'left of' the new one
Interval starts at or before the new one's end, so it overlaps (given it isn't left of it)
Grows the new interval to cover the overlap
Slice from i, appended in one go

p: `intervals = [[1,2],[3,5],[6,7],[8,10],[12,16]]`, `new = [4,8]`. The input is sorted, so the intervals fall into three consecutive groups.

blocks.h: Why two separate while loops instead of one with ifs?
p: The sorted order guarantees the three groups are contiguous: first all intervals fully left, then all that overlap, then all fully right. Two loops walk that structure directly, with a single shared index `i`, and the merged interval is appended exactly once between the groups.

bullets: Time: O(n), one pass with no sorting needed since the input is already sorted.
Space: O(n) for the result.

p: Touching intervals count as overlapping (`<=`), e.g. `[1,2]` and `[2,3]` merge into `[1,3]`; the first loop uses strict `<` for the same reason.

57.takeaway: Insert into sorted intervals with three phases: copy the ones before, merge the overlapping ones, copy the ones after.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: One row of path counts; the start has exactly one path
2-D grid DP that only needs the previous row
No path can pass through a blocked cell
Before the line `dp[j]` still holds the count from the cell above, `dp[j-1]` is the count from the left (already updated); their sum is the new count
Last element = paths to the bottom-right cell

p: Grid with an obstacle in the middle. After each cell, `dp` holds the path counts for the current row (cells to the right of `j` still show the previous row's values):

blocks.h: Why can one row of dp replace the whole table?
p: Each cell depends only on the cell above (the old `dp[j]`) and the cell to the left (`dp[j-1]`, already refreshed this row). Scanning left to right keeps exactly those two values available, so earlier rows can be forgotten.

bullets: Time: O(m·n).
Space: O(n), a single row.
If the start (`g[0][0]`) is an obstacle, the first cell sets `dp[0]` to 0 and everything after stays 0, so the answer is correctly 0.

63.takeaway: Grid-path DP with a rolling row: new count = from above + from left, zeroed on obstacles.
